Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) serves as a privacy-preserving machine learning technique designed to facilitate knowledge sharing among data-silent parties without compromising user privacy. However, current research suggests that V parties remain vulnerable to privacy breaches. This study introduces the concept of "practical privacy" within the VFL context, which evaluates the likelihood that a party can successfully infer sensitive information from another party's data. Our findings demonstrate that under specific conditions, particularly when data distributions align, participants can inadvertently reveal sensitive information to adversaries. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach known as "pragmatic privacy" and develop a novel method called "pragmatic learning." Pragmatic learning ensures that model parameters remain consistent regardless of the input data, thereby preventing information leakage. Experimental results confirm that this approach significantly enhances privacy protection while simultaneously maintaining high model accuracy.

The study examines the semileptonic $B$-meson decay process leading to a baryon and a corresponding dark antibaryon. Utilizing the QCD light-cone sum rules (QCD LCSR) framework, the form factors associated with this decay are derived. The analysis further evaluates mass splitting and charge asymmetry within the context of a simplified "dark sector" model.

This paper introduces the "Intelligent Urban Defense Game," a novel approach to training urban defenders against intelligent Socio-Cyber-Physical Threats (SCPTs) by integrating advanced AI and Game Theory. Unlike traditional models that treat cities as static spaces or rely on basic AI and random tactics, our system employs AI-driven Game Theory to optimize resource deployment. Specifically, the system selects the optimal location for urban defense resources to maximize the minimum utility achieved against an adaptive SCPT opponent, which utilizes reinforcement learning to maximize its own payoff. This dynamic interaction creates a complex, non-linear, and stochastic optimization challenge. To address this, we propose a hybrid AI solution combining Game Theory with Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). The resulting framework significantly outperforms existing methods, including random strategies and other advanced AI models, in terms of both training efficiency and real-world deployment.

We investigate the thermodynamics of "black stars" within a finite cavity situated in asymptotically flat spacetime, focusing on their phase transition characteristics. Our findings reveal that these black stars possess a minimum size; if the cavity is smaller than this critical value, a stable black star cannot form. When the cavity exceeds this threshold, we identify a transition from a normal star to a black star as the cavity's volume increases. Furthermore, by analyzing black holes with a radius of curvature significantly larger than their event horizon, we observe a Hawking–Page phase transition between black stars and normal stars.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant force in graph-based machine learning, yet their reliance on abundant labeled data often proves difficult to secure. To address this, we introduce PseudoTAG, a pseudo-labeling method designed to enhance GNN training on datasets with scarce annotations. Unlike traditional approaches, PseudoTAG mitigates issues arising from class imbalance and low model confidence by employing a dual-criteria filter. This method ensures that generated labels are not only reliable but also informative, focusing specifically on edges that are critical for connectivity within the graph. Experimental results across various real-world benchmarks demonstrate that P TAG consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art pseudo-labeling techniques.

In the initial phase of AWAKE Run 2, a proton beam dump incident produced extensive amounts of secondary radiation, including neutrons, gamma rays, and photons of various energies. Among these, betatron X-rays present a distinct risk due to their high penetrating power, a factor that demands careful attention for radiation safety. This study simulates proton-electron interactions occurring within the main undulator employed in the dump area to analyze the properties of this specific emission. We evaluate the probability of photon generation across different beam parameters and project the corresponding dose rates within the experiment's peripheral zones. Furthermore, we assess the potential for these X-rays to penetrate deeply into the underground facility, specifically reaching the target interaction point of the ESS (Electron-Spontaneous Synchrotron) or similar high-energy experiments, should such penetration occur.

Differentially private decision tree learning is a vital technique for mining sensitive data, yet current methods struggle to produce trees that are both deep enough and stable under privacy constraints. This paper introduces two new algorithms for computing differentially private decision trees: DP-HIST and DP-BST. These approaches are the first to rigorously demonstrate privacy preservation, offering provable guarantees of differential privacy. DP-HIST is a straightforward method that adapts existing private histogram computation to adjust the private histogram threshold, thereby balancing tree depth and differential privacy. In contrast, DP-BST leverages a novel, depth-adaptive rounding strategy within a binary space tree to achieve more precise differentially private predictions. Experimental results indicate that DP-HIST generates stable differentially private trees with controlled depths, while DP-BST delivers superior classification accuracy compared to existing methods.

This study addresses the challenge of defining a distance metric for probability distributions that remains robust even when calculations involve only tail or head regions of the distributions. To this end, we propose the R\'enyi distance, an extension of the R\'enyi entropy concept, which is defined through the Kullback-Leibler divergence and incorporates a region-specific parameter $\alpha$. We analyze the behavior of this metric across various scenarios and demonstrate its utility in two applications: comparing the performance of different machine learning models and analyzing the structural properties of distributions themselves. Furthermore, we introduce a regularized variant of the distance and develop a back-proximal gradient algorithm designed to compute the minimizer of an appropriate regularized objective.

Chain Event Networks (ChENs) serve as a non-parametric extension of event chains, utilizing transition probabilities to model the dynamics of time series data. While standard event chain analysis typically estimates all parameters as a single integrated event sequence, Chain Event Networks allow for distinct parameter estimation at each temporal step. This flexibility is advantageous for capturing time-varying data characteristics but introduces the challenge of excessive parameter counting, which can result in overfitting. To address this, we present a Bayesian selection framework that determines the optimal number of parameters for estimation at every stage of the ChEN structure. Our approach relies on a prior predictive model comparison strategy, which is applied iteratively across all time points to guide this selection process. Empirical validation using both simulated datasets and real-world examples demonstrates that the proposed method effectively mitigates overfitting.

Adhesion to surfaces is vital for mobile barrier adhering robots, which traverse irregular and dynamic obstacles such as those in mine environments. These robots are often actuated by suction cups or adhesive pads, and their motion is controlled by adjusting the internal pressure within these elements. However, when the internal pressure is insufficient to maintain the pads against mine obstacles, the pads can detach, causing the robot to deviate from its intended path. This study examines the relationship between pressure levels and pad detachment, and the resulting robot movement. We present a novel theoretical framework for analyzing this phenomenon and validate it through experimental results.

Although recent advancements in generative growth have enabled the creation of stunning organic structures, their application to biological organisms remains restricted. This limitation stems from the scarcity of tools that facilitate biological discovery, as well as the significant challenges posed by the intricate interplay between growth dynamics and spatial constraints. To address this, we introduce GrowSpace, a comprehensive framework that equips users with the ability to formulate hypotheses, test them through simulation, and iteratively refine their insights into plant development. Our system offers an accessible entry point for non-experts to explore plant biology via visual feedback loops and provides specific insights into GrowSpace's design, a botanical catalog, and associated visual analytics. Through the distribution of the system's web-based prototype to a broad user base, we gathered diverse feedback that highlights its potential and identifies avenues for further improvement.

This study establishes a complete characterization of the stochastic Loewner evolution (SLE) cycle for $\kappa \in (0, 4)$, achieved by defining a specific probability measure on the space of $(-1)$-cut SLE$_\kappa$ paths starting at $-1$ and terminating at $1$ within the unit disk. A realization of this measure is constructed through a "random conormal gluing" method using quantum disks, where the boundary identification function is defined as a Bessel process of index $-\frac{2}{\kappa}$. The findings indicate that the cycle is formed by independently chordal SLE$_\kappa$ paths connecting the boundary points $-1$ and $1$ across each cut interval, with connections made at the respective cut endpoints.

This study examines the contributions of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances to strange baryon production in photonic interactions involving a nucleon, utilizing a dynamical model that incorporates non-resonant terms and s-channel resonances. By analyzing photonic cross-sections and $\pi^0\pi^0$ production rates, the research identifies that these higher-spin states make a significant impact on the photonic cross-section within the 1.6 to 1.8 GeV center-of-mass energy range, specifically influencing the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ production channels. Conversely, the $T\pi^0\pi^0$ production cross-section shows minimal sensitivity to these nuclear and delta-like resonances. The findings are juxtaposed against experimental data from MAMI, JLab, and SINC, with a particular focus on the $K\Sigma$ photonic cross-section. The analysis reveals a notable discrepancy between the calculated non-resonant background and experimental observations at energies exceeding 1.8 GeV for the $K\Sigma$ production channel.

This paper details the application of the OpenCV toolkit to pre-treat images from the MORPH-II dataset. As a comprehensive collection of nearly 15,000 faces, MORPH II is renowned for its high quality and diversity, though it retains valuable characteristics even after applying specific enhancements. In this work, we employ OpenCV to execute various image pre-treatment operations, including color correction, brightness and contrast adjustments, along with enhancements to clarity and sharpness.

We demonstrate that a curvaton decaying into an ancient black hole (ABH) offers a viable mechanism for generating primordial black holes. This scenario is particularly attractive because the ABH abundance can serve as a proxy for curvaton-driven inflation. We examine the evolution of the ABH population and calculate their present-day mass fraction. Furthermore, we assess the impact of these primordial black holes on the cosmic microwave background, the abundance of existing ancient black holes, and the production of gravitational waves. Finally, we outline future research directions and the broader implications of this framework.

This study introduces a novel method for educational pathway analysis by employing a latent variable model grounded in a new representation of educational pathways as partially ordered sets. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on counting pathway occurrences, this approach calculates pathway probabilities using uniform distribution across all possible routes between a student's entry and exit points, thereby distributing weight according route popularity. Our pathway data is collected directly from institution records, removing the reliance on student interviews or surveys. Consequently, we bypass biases stemming from recall errors or student subjective preferences. By applying the proposed algorithm, we transform raw pathway data into a bias-free, high-dimensional space that facilitates robust modeling. The paper presents the pathway model using a Probit framework, where admission probabilities are conditioned on student characteristics. Our analysis confirms that this proposed method yields insights comparable to those derived from conventional popularity-based approaches.

This study introduces a novel differential game framework to govern the formation of autonomous vehicle platoons, wherein each vehicle acts as an independent agent attempting to reach a predefined formation in coordination with others. Modeled as a cooperative differential game, each vehicle optimizes its trajectory to achieve this shared goal while minimizing a personal cost function. The proposed mechanism incorporates a link-based interaction model, allowing agents to exchange state data only when physically adjacent, thereby conserving communication bandwidth and enhancing security. Furthermore, to ensure robustness against communication delays, a discrete event trigger is implemented, ensuring that continuous data exchange occurs only when necessary based on specific conditions. The article derives sufficient conditions for the solvability of the differential equation and proves the asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system. Simulation results demonstrate that the developed control strategy successfully achieves stable platoons formation while significantly reducing unnecessary communication events.

This study addresses interaction effects within logistic regression. We introduce a new method to quantify interaction strength, establish a limit for additive logistic regression models, and develop an additive approach to incorporate interaction into these models. We also propose a new class of interaction terms that encompass both multiplicative and additive forms. We derive the asymptotic distribution of the additive estimator and provide a heuristic for its variance reduction. Finally, we suggest a model selection strategy and demonstrate its efficacy through numerical examples.

Headline detection involves identifying the main claim within a given text, a notoriously difficult task for Natural Language Processing systems due to its reliance on deep understanding. In this study, we introduce a new automatic headline creation method that leverages Transformer models, specifically exploring how varying architectural choices and training strategies impact performance. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the HEADLINES challenge dataset, utilizing a BERT-based model enhanced with attention mechanisms and a content-based filtering layer to focus on relevant details. By further analyzing how these architectural decisions influence outcomes, we offer key insights for future research in automatic headline generation.

Spin-orbit coupling in materials lacking inversion symmetry enables the generation of chiral spin textures and dynamic states through electric fields. This study demonstrates that chiral spin fluids can emerge in both amorphous and polycrystalline alloys utilizing a weak, tunable spin-orbit coupling mechanism driven by the Rashba effect. Specifically, within a disordered quantum wire framework, we utilize a first-principles-calibrated effective Hamiltonian to simulate the evolution of spin configurations under an external electric field. Our findings reveal that amorphous and polycrystalline systems exhibit a transition between a uniform helical configuration and a domain-rich state characterized by a non-zero spin Hall conductivity. Additionally, we identify a distinct regime producing a quasi-localized spin Hall effect. Ultimately, these results establish a practical route to engineering chiral spin fluids and spin Hall currents in low-cost, low-quality crystalline structures.

Radio interferometers are essential tools for high-resolution astronomy, yet their potential is constrained by random phase fluctuations caused by the Earth's atmosphere and minor inconsistencies between antenna phase centers. To recover the true sky signal, interferometric data must be calibrated. This process involves determining and correcting for these phase variations, a task typically performed by cross-correlating signals from all antenna pairs. In a system with $N$ antennas, this brute-force method requires $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ computations, which becomes a significant bottleneck for current and future large-scale arrays. This paper proposes a hybrid algorithm that combines the standard cross-correlation technique with a Fourier transform-based approach. By leveraging a regular grid layout of antennas, this new strategy reduces the computational complexity to $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})}$, representing a substantial efficiency improvement. The effectiveness of this method was validated using both simulated datasets and real-world radio astronomy observations.

This study introduces a new automatic portfolio allocation approach leveraging an adaptive generative conditional adversarial network (GCGAN). The GCGAN framework enables the synthesis of portfolios exhibiting predefined risk-return profiles, thereby facilitating a more extensive exploration of the efficient frontier. The methodology was evaluated using historical market data, demonstrating that an appropriately designed Investment Portfolio (IP) can yield superior returns with reduced exposure to downside risk. The results further indicate that the framework effectively isolates the impacts of market dynamics and individual asset behaviors on final portfolio performance.

This study introduces a Bayesian neural network designed to classify active galactic nuclei (AGN) and quasars using gamma-ray data from the Fermi-LAT, leveraging spectral properties to differentiate them. The model was trained on a dataset of 1,043 quasars and 1,043 blazars, each characterized by 11 gamma-ray spectral parameters. It was subsequently tested on a sample of 1,043 blazars, 1,043 Seyfert galaxies, and 1,043 starburst galaxies, employing the same 11 parameters for each class. The results indicate that the Bayesian neural network successfully distinguishes between the two primary subcategories of AGN—blazars and Seyfert galaxies—with 99% accuracy for blazars and 95% for Seyfergs. It also achieves 99% classification accuracy for the starburst galaxies. These findings suggest that the Bayesian approach is well-suited for modeling the probability distributions of the input data.

This study examines the obstacles and opportunities hindering web-based social media content authors from making their media fully accessible. Through a survey of 100 participants, the research highlights a lack of awareness regarding best practices for creating accessible content across digital platforms. Additionally, individuals often feel constrained by a combination of personal, financial, technical, and knowledge-based factors when attempting to produce inclusive social media material. Consequently, the paper outlines specific strategies to empower social media creators in generating a wider variety of accessible content.

A concept study was conducted to evaluate the scientific potential of a proposed space-based observatory for India, named INSIST. Designed as a versatile facility capable of both high-resolution spectroscopy and wide-field imaging, it would operate across ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared wavelengths. With a 1.2-meter aperture, it offers capabilities complementary to existing and planned international missions, specifically addressing the unique scientific requirements of the Indian astronomy community. This report outlines the rationale for the project, detailing its proposed scientific objectives, instrument specifications, and overall system design.

This study introduces a novel statistical technique for analyzing continuous clinical trial data in Alzheimer's research by leveraging a nonparametric estimator that captures the Efficacy Time (ET) and Duration of Efficacy (DLE) as functions of administered drug dosage. The primary objective is to estimate a smooth, continuous relationship between drug levels and clinical trial outcomes. The proposed methodology utilizes natural cubic splines to model this dose-response connection, with the number and placement of spline knots determined via a data-driven algorithm. The approach was validated using simulations and subsequently applied to an ongoing Phase IIb clinical trial evaluating the antiamyloid drug BAN2401 in patients with mild-to-moderate disease. The results indicate a statistically significant positive correlation between drug dosage and both ET and DLE metrics.

We introduce a novel technique for enhancing the likelihood of observing rare events by employing an optimization-based strategy. This method amplifies events that require the least effort, as evaluated by a designated cost function. In recent years, the widespread availability of pre-trained models has spurred the development of powerful, data-driven solutions for various computer vision tasks. However, a critical limitation remains: these models often struggle to adapt to new classes when undergoing ongoing learning. This challenge is particularly pronounced in image recognition scenarios where the distribution of data for the newly introduced classes differs significantly from that of the original pre-trained model's training set. To address this gap, we introduce a basic benchmark that specifically targets the ongoing learning capabilities of pre-trained models. This benchmark emphasizes scalability by allowing an unlimited number of new classes to be added sequentially. Experimental results demonstrate that even state-of-the-art deep neural networks fail to effectively learn from these newly added classes. Consequently, we argue that this issue warrants further investigation and that our proposed benchmark serves as a vital step toward that goal.

Social media content is frequently multi-modal, containing both text and images. Magnetospheric Axion-Io-IAXO, a proposed next-generation X-ray telescope, is designed to investigate the Sun's interior through heliospheric axion searches. By leveraging its large effective aperture, BabyIAXO aims to enhance sensitivity specifically for solar regions near the photosphere and center. This study employs a detailed model of the Sun, utilizing both the BSS93 model and observations from SOHO/MDI, to assess the region of maximum conversion probability for photons into axions near the center. We analyze how this probability depends on the sound speed and density profiles, as well as the sound speed gradient at that location. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the magnetic field geometry and strength on the maximum probability. Our results indicate that for plausible parameter ranges, the region of peak photon-to-axion conversion is located within 0.95 to 0.96 solar radii from the center. Additionally, we evaluate the sensitivity of BabyIAXO to solar center axions, demonstrating that X-ray telescopes can probe a broader range of axion masses compared to gamma-ray instruments.

Grasping is a critical and essential capability for any object manipulation system. However, the vast variety of shapes and sizes of real-world objects makes it nearly impossible to exhaustively cover all scenarios through physical experimentation alone. This limitation is further exacerbated by the challenges of deploying physical robots in uncontrolled environments. To address these issues, this study introduces **DexGraspNet**, a comprehensive dataset comprising 100,000 diverse grasps across 1,000 object categories. DexGraspNet is generated using the MuJoCo-based HMPG simulator, which models a 7-DOF KUKA arm interacting with a 3D-rendered environment. By aggregating data across varied object categories, the dataset enables the development of robust grasping algorithms that generalize well to unseen objects. The dataset is created via a specialized generation pipeline that simulates the object placement process, resulting in a 7-DOF grasping configuration for each item. The resulting data is formatted as JSON objects, where each item contains a grasp definition along with its corresponding 7-DOF parameters. The robustness of the generated distribution is further validated by its compatibility with the YCB-Objects dataset, which includes 64 diverse objects and their associated 7-DOF grasps. The full dataset can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/zhengyongchen/DexGraspNet.

This study introduces an innovative, free-breathing 4D (3D+respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MRI technique, optimized for a broad range of patients and resistant to respiratory artifacts. Our method relies on a motion-compensation strategy that integrates respiratory signal monitoring with prospective motion correction. The system captures respiratory data using two auxiliary 1D coils during the initial 10 of a 120-s scan duration. The primary dataset, acquired in 120 segments, is then sorted into four distinct groups based on the recorded respiratory signals. Subsequently, prospective motion correction is applied to each group, aligning the k-space data within every single 120-s frame to account for breathing movements. The final output is a 4D (3D+breathing) T2-weighted image set. Validation was performed on 10 patients, including six children and four adults, to assess the method's efficacy. The results demonstrate that this approach delivers high-quality, motion-compensated anatomical images of the abdomen, pelvis, and thorax without requiring breath-holds or sedation.

Knowledge distillation (KD) represents a leading technique for compressing deep neural networks (DNNs) by transferring knowledge from a large teacher model to a compact student model. However, most current KD approaches disregard the application's specific data flows, resulting in suboptimal performance. This paper presents in Distill, a data-flow-aware KD framework designed to maintain the structural data flows of the student model while distilling information from a teacher. Distinct from conventional methods that rely on layer-to-layer mapping, Distill employs data-flow-preserving (DFP) projection layers to establish multiple, flexible mappings between teacher and student architectures. These layers adaptively select the most beneficial mappings based on the input data to maximize distillation efficacy. Empirical evaluations across various classification and object detection tasks demonstrate that Distill consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-reduce methods.

This paper outlines a proof-of-concept proof that elevates running quantum algorithms, specifically the Altman and Wootens' 2000 Quantum Prisoner's Dilemma, from local execution to a remote quantum cloud. We demonstrate how this transition enables secure access, facilitates collaboration, and supports hybrid quantum-classical workflows. Our results indicate that raising the qubit frequency is a vital optimization tactic that significantly improves result accuracy. Consequently, we conclude that frequency-traded elevations are essential for executing quantum algorithms reliably on cloud infrastructure.

We investigate a two-tier market where a seller supplies a product to a buyer, mediated by an intermediary who operates without profit motive. Focusing on a risk-neutral agent who must secure a specific good, we demonstrate that the presence of this middleperson alters the risk strategy of the seller. Consequently, the distribution of wealth and the mechanisms for acquisition shift, directly impacting the risk-exposed party's financial expectations. We further establish that, as risk aversion increases, the likelihood of an intermediary facilitating a transaction rises, while their anticipated earnings decline. Finally, we analyze a scenario where the intermediary possesses income generation capabilities independent of facilitating deals. We find that even with the option to generate revenue through independent work, the agent's total expected earnings remain higher when they successfully facilitate a transaction than in the absence thereof.

Summarizing structured data involves two distinct phases: first, identifying the relevant information subsets, and second, reconstructing that data into a coherent narrative. While neural models have achieved success in reconstructive summarizing of relational tables, they often fail to generalize well across diverse real-world datasets. We introduce a two-stage approach called Planning with Acquired Entity Promises (AEP). In the first stage, the system plans the information retrieval by querying the table and generating queries, which are then executed to return a list of pertinent entities. In the second stage, the system generates the final summary sentences by conditioning on this list of entities. We hypothesize that transforming entity lists into natural language prompts enhances the generative capabilities of decoders. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Furthermore, we present criteria characterizing the generalized differentiability of multivariate functions in a manner analogous to the implications of class one status, specifically leveraging the behavior of their restrictions to lower-dimensional subspaces.

Vocal entrainment, the unconscious synchronization of speech patterns between conversing individuals, serves as a key indicator of social bonding and is also utilized strategically to build rapport. To date, the majority of investigations into this phenomenon have examined rapid, back-and-forch exchanges such as laughter or pauses. In contrast, our study investigates vocal entrainment within longer utterances during natural dyadic dialogues. We introduce a new approach that measures the temporal and acoustic similarities of complete words spoken sequentially by two participants. Applied to authentic conversation data, this method demonstrates that speakers subtly align their vocal characteristics with those of their dialogue partner in real time.

This study introduces a novel approach to quantum control leveraging Lambda-S1 within the quantum domain. Lambda-S1 serves as an alternative to D-Wire, offering a more efficient framework for quantum regulation. We demonstrate that D-Wire can be effectively reformulated using D-Lambda-S1 structures, thereby enhancing the quantum control process. To further enhance the clarity of this methodology, we establish a categorical framework for D-Lambda-S1, providing a robust foundation for analyzing and constructing D-Lambda-S1 systems. This work marks a significant advancement in the field of quantum regulation.

This evidence suggests that star-driven outflows play a critical role in regulating and suppressing star formation in M82.

We evaluate the utility of pre-training with monocular depth estimation compared to image classification for tasks like semantic segmentation. Our findings indicate that, particularly in the context of limited labeled data, the self-supervised, monocular approach yields segmentation accuracy comparable to or superior to self-supervised pre-training. Additionally, we demonstrate that this method remains highly effective even when combined with standard supervised classification pre-training. Finally, we present a practical, end-to-end trained model that achieves competitive results on the Cityscapes dataset.

A fundamental challenge in Bayesian nonparametrics involves estimating the unknown dependence structure of a multivariate distribution using Kendall's tau. Although this estimator performs well in many contexts, it suffers from an inability to produce valid lower bounds because its sampling distribution is asymmetric around the true parameter value. To address this limitation, we introduce an effective deducing method that achieves formal, valid coverage. Through extensive simulation testing across diverse scenarios, the proposed approach demonstrates robust and reliable performance.

This paper introduces a novel framework for ensuring data privacy within automotive networks, specifically through the use of collaborative edge cognitive systems. As autonomous vehicles (AVs) increasingly rely on edge cognitive systems to process data locally, they also gain the capacity to perform sensitive learning tasks on behalf of users. However, existing systems lack adequate protection against the leakage of private information. To address this gap, we propose a new collaborative edge cognitive architecture that combines Multi-Knowledge Distillation (KTD) with Differential Privacy (DP). This approach allows the system to extract and transfer only the essential knowledge required for effective learning, while simultaneously applying DP techniques to prevent the leakage of private data during the transfer process. Furthermore, we developed an adaptive mechanism to automatically determine the optimal level of DP noise. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches by achieving superior accuracy while better preserving user privacy.

We introduce a technique for extracting and analyzing Euler curves within significant surfaces. This approach is applied to Euler surfaces arising from the quadratic forms of slices in the data cube, offering novel insights into the patterns of clusters and validating the statistical importance of these surfaces. We further examine surfaces linked to data-driven models, specifically examining the quadrupole of a Gaussian mixture model alongside the level sets of a neural network's output. Additionally, we discuss how the topology of significance surfaces can be leveraged to detect anomalies in cluster numbers and estimate outliers.

This study examines an autonomous, smooth, and non-autonomous system featuring a significant Allee effect, modeled as a predator-prey dynamics with the following differential equations:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{x} &= r x \left(1 - \frac{x}{K}\right)\left(\frac{x - x_0}{K - K_0}\right) - \frac{ax^2}{x^2 + m^2}y, \\
\dot{y} &= c y \left(1 - \frac{y}{L}\right) - \frac{bx^2}{x^2 + m^2}y,
\end{aligned}
$$
where $x$ and $y$ represent the population densities of the predator and prey, respectively, and the parameters are positive constants. The analysis focuses on the long-term behavior of the system, particularly the influence of the Allee effect on the existence, stability, and multiplicity of interior equilibria. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the system exhibits an interior equilibrium that is globally asymptotically stable, provided that the predator's functional response follows a Holling type-IV curve. Furthermore, we establish that the positive phase portrait is bounded and invariant under the condition that the predator's growth rate is sufficiently low relative to the prey's carrying capacity. Finally, we illustrate these theoretical findings with numerical simulations.

In this paper, we investigate the on-line aspect pivot (AP) method for solving linear optimization problems. For any linear optimization problem where the objective function is strictly increasing, we demonstrate that the algorithm's iteration sequence is bounded away from the problem feasible region's asymptotic directions. These directions represent feasible rays where the objective function is unbounded in the upward direction. Furthermore, we establish that the sequence of objective function values produced by AP converges monotonically toward the optimal value. Additionally, we prove convergence to the global optimum under the assumption of finite solutions, provided a mild condition holds: the algorithm must not become trapped cycling indefinitely at a local optimum. Finally, we show that the sequence of search points generated by AP accumulates at global solutions whenever they exist.

This study investigates off-shell jets within $t\bar{t}j$ events at the LHC, employing a weight-based method to extract the top quark mass. We analyze the influence of these off-shell jets on the determined value using both Monte Carlo simulations and real LHC data. Our analysis indicates that the influence of these jets is negligible, with an associated systematic uncertainty of 0.1 GeV.

This study examines Vision Transformers (ViTs) as a tool for face anti-spoofing and detection, specifically within a lossless state. We demonstrate that these models can learn the necessary features for detection even without annotated data, surpassing previous research that relied on dataless fine-tuning. Furthermore, we offer a theoretical framework explaining why ViTs remain effective in this lossless data scenario. To support these claims, we introduce the VT-FAS dataset, the largest publicly available collection of Vision Transformer data for face spoofing detection. This dataset includes 10 widely used liveness challenges and covers 50 diverse identities.

Autonomous vehicles represent a highly complex and multifaceted challenge in the realm of self-driving technology. To address this complexity, we introduce Profound Reinforcement Learning (PRL), an innovative system designed to enhance self-driving capabilities. The PRL framework integrates three core components: a system-level information system (SLIS), a RL-based decision-making engine (RMDM), and a deep learning (DL) model (DLM). The DLM processes visual and sensor data to generate an output, which the RMDM utilizes to determine the vehicle's trajectory. Concurrently, the SLIS monitors the interaction between the agent and its environment, evaluating a multi-dimensional reward structure that encompasses safety, efficiency, and legal adherence. By combining these subsystems, the PRL architecture successfully navigated the difficult "Highway" and "Highway Hard" environments of the Neural Network Driving (NNDL) benchmark, achieving top-tier performance. Furthermore, the architecture demonstrated robust adaptability when tested on the Autonomous Driving Challenge (ADC) platform, with results anticipated to be published in forthcoming publications.

Parallelization is a common strategy for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) to mitigate the computational demands of parallel processing. However, asynchronous parallel execution, often favored for its implementation simplicity, can introduce evaluation-time biases. This paper presents a new parent selection mechanism designed to reduce such biases by prioritizing solutions based on their frequency of asynchronous selection rather than the sequential order of their evaluation. Additionally, a frequency-aware completion stopping criterion is proposed to enhance the efficiency of asynchronous parallel MOEAs. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed selection strategy, along with the custom stopping criterion, effectively mitigates evaluation-time biases in both criteria.

The ongoing surge in microlensing planet discoveries has been driven by the extensive, long-term monitoring of the Galactic bulge by the OGLE survey. This study presents the confirmation of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, the 100th planet found via microlensing and the 29th such world located in the Galactic disk. We utilized three nights of adaptive optics-assisted microlensing observations from the Keck I telescope to achieve this validation. The resulting planet-host separation of $1.09 \pm 0.06$ AU and mass of $3.1 \pm 0.3$ M$_\oplus$ are robust against adaptive lenses that magnify the source region by up to 16 times. Notably, the high degree of source image saturation in OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 makes this a prime example of the Kepler lensing advantage for characterizing planets within a few AU of their hosts. Furthermore, this planet is the coldest confirmed microlensing exoplanet to date, with an equilibrium temperature of 174 K.

We establish that an asymptotic series for solutions to the Lindblad equation, characterized by time-regular components, exists under conditions where the initial state and Lindblad operators possess specific analytic properties. The governing dynamics are expressed as $i\dot{\rho}_t = [H,\rho_t] + \sum_{k}\Gamma_s[\Gamma_s,\rho_t]_+$, where the superoperator $\Gamma_s := \frac{1}{2}(G_s^\dagger G_s + G_s^\dagger G_s)$ corresponds to a coupling operator $G_s$. The Hamiltonian $H$ is assumed to be time-regular, defined as $\sum_{k=0}^N i^k \partial_t^k H$, with the Lindblad operators sharing this regularity property. The study demonstrates the existence of a high-rate asymptotic series for the solution, with its leading term being the initial state $\rho_0$. This result extends previous work by demonstrating the feasibility of such expansions for systems subject to rapid temporal variations in their parameters.

This study examines CePd$_1$$-$$x$$Rh$$x$$ alloys using neutron depolarization measurements, revealing that a partial randomization of Ce spins arises from both spin disorder and spin blocking effects. The degree of spin disordering correlates with the volume fraction of Ce$^{3+}$ ions, a state driven by the Ce$^{3+}$-Ce$^{4+}$ exchange interaction. Conversely, the onset of spin blocking occurs at low temperatures within Ce ions adjacent to Rh atoms, stemming from the Ce$$-$$Rh exchange coupling and the restricted movement of Ce spin due to Rh spin. The findings are interpreted through a model where depolarization signals result from the combined influence of Ce$$-$$Rh exchange interaction and spin fluidity.

Within the context of $\beta$-computation theory, this study introduces a new class of intermediaries that arise during algorithmic $\beta$-reduction. These reductions occur specifically when $\beta$-reduction algorithms prioritize $\beta$-reduction steps separated by a specific numerical interval, denoted as a *gap*, from the current Redex (a specific location for reduction). These gaps are a defining feature of $\beta$-reduction algorithms operating in normal mode. Consequently, our findings have significant implications for understanding $\beta$-reduction algorithms operating on normal forms.

To substantiate this, we define a novel meta-relation called *transfer* and demonstrate that it encompasses the newly discovered intermediate $\beta$-computation steps. Furthermore, we prove that intermediate $\beta$-computation steps occurring on normal forms are greedy transfers occurring with a specified gap. As a corollary, we establish that any algorithm operating on normal forms—provided it only executes $\beta$-reduction steps via single $\beta$-transfers in a greedy manner—is guaranteed to be convergent. This result constitutes a fresh proof of the validity of the Barendregt, van der Woude, and van der Woude proof regarding the confluence of $\beta$-computation.

The study of the rare decay process $B_s \to J/\psi\pi\pi$ offers a unique avenue for investigating potential Standard Model violations. By analyzing data from 36.7 inverse femtobarns of $pp$ collisions collected by the LHCb detector, researchers reconstructed three specific final states: $J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$, along with two resonant configurations of $J/\psi\pi\pi$ involving $f_0(500)^0$ and $f_0(1000)^0$ resonances. The analysis focused on the angular distribution of the $B_s$ decay, specifically looking for deviations from the predictions of the Standard Model. To achieve this, a CP-violating phase, denoted as $\phi_s$, was extracted using the amplitude analysis technique. The results yielded a measurement of $\phi_s = -0.03 \pm 0.11 \pm 0.06$ radians for the channel involving $J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$ resonant states, which translates to a 1.1 sigma deviation from the Standard Model expectation of zero. The corresponding significance for the non-resonant $J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$ channel was calculated to be 1.3 sigma.

Domain migration stands as a pivotal concept within machine learning, enabling models trained on one domain to function effectively in another. This study examines migration strategies for the specific task of identifying aerial imagery, comparing their efficacy against both cross-validation and retraining baselines using a case-based approach. The analysis reveals that, for general image classification, cross-validation and retraining often outperform the investigated domain migration techniques. Nevertheless, these methods remain valuable by offering the utility of a model that circumvents the need to retrain or handle validation data from the target domain.

This study explores the enumeration of arcs within the two-dimensional space over a finite field, $\mathbb F_q^2$. We establish an algorithm capable of enumerating all arcs of any specified length in polynomial time relative to $O(q^2 \ell q)$. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach for enumerating arcs of specific lengths using recursive techniques in $O(q^2 \ell q)$. Arc enumeration serves as a critical component for generating combinatorial designs, particularly designs of the type $(v, 2, \lambda) t$. Furthermore, we outline an algorithm for constructing such designs in $O(v^2 t)$. These algorithms are implemented in the Python-based `xeer` library, accessible via the provided link.

This study presents an investigation into the effectiveness of a non-verbal reasoning demonstration. Participants were tasked with identifying triangles within a structured array of squares. The experiment involved two phases: 100 individuals completed an initial phase without prior instruction, while another 20 underwent a second phase that included viewing a tutorial explaining the task's rationale before making a decision. The findings indicate that pre-existing knowledge significantly enhances reasoning performance. Specifically, individuals who received explanatory guidance were able to solve the task in 10% of the time required by those who did not, solving it in merely 10 versus 100 units respectively. The results suggest that while individuals can deduce a task's purpose and underlying logic through observation alone, providing explicit verbal explanations further accelerates this process. The study concludes by offering recommendations for the creation of tasks that facilitate more efficient non-verbal reasoning.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become essential tools for machine learning tasks involving graph data, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by high computational costs and barriers to domain adoption. To address this, we introduce a graph neural network parameterized approach that replaces dynamic message passing with equivalent fixed-size neural networks. This transformation yields two primary advantages: it drastically reduces computational overhead and simplifies the model into a static structure that standard neural network training algorithms can handle. We demonstrate that this method is both general and efficient, offering speedups of up to 100-fold compared to original GNN models while maintaining high predictive accuracy.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the RXCJ0232.2-4420 cluster, which includes new X-ray data from *XMM-Newton* and *Chandra*, alongside archival data from *ROSAT*, *Chandra*, and *XMM-Newton*. Our study reveals that the cluster hosts a central galaxy, RXCJ0232.2-4420A, characterized by a bright radio lobe and a radio-loud AGN. This AGN is situated within a subcluster located in the southern part of the system. Our findings indicate that RXCJ0232.2-4420A is a Perseus-type cD galaxy, distinguished by a steep X-ray profile gradient in its southern region caused by the AGN's interaction with the intracluster medium. This interaction demonstrates that the radio lobes have moved through the southern subcluster material, resulting in the formation of a radio relic and triggering a shock wave. Consequently, RXCJ0232.2-4420A is identified as a member of the southern subcluster rather than the main cluster core. This discovery indicates that the current configuration of RXCJ0232.2-4420.2 represents a merging scenario between RXCJ0232.2-4420A and the southern subcluster.

Legend Memory Modules (LeMM) serve as a memory component within deep learning frameworks, designed to model long-term dependencies and enhance recurrent networks. Although LeMMs are theoretically simple, their efficiency is currently compromised by non-linear operations in the memory kernel that require sequential execution. This limitation becomes a significant bottleneck when LeMMs are deployed in large language models, which necessitate thousands of parameters. To address this, we introduce a novel parallelized training algorithm capable of accelerating LeMM learning. This method allows for the simultaneous computation previously restricted by sequential steps. We have integrated this algorithm into the LLaMA framework to enable the pre-training of LeMM-enhanced models at scale. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields performance improvements equivalent to standard LLaMA while reducing training time by a factor of four.

Weakly-Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) have been the primary focus of the search for Dark Matter for several decades, yet experimental results continue to show no evidence. This persistent nullification has prompted the community to explore alternative solutions, including both lighter, non-nucleonic particles and those with interactions beyond the weak force. This overview outlines current progress in Weakly-Interacting Particle Dark Matter research, covering both established experiments and emerging proposals.

We demonstrate that a two-person, symmetric, zero-sum game with transferable costs, where participants can freely enter or exit, serves as a framework for analyzing the evolution of communication. This model simulates a "labeling game" with two competing labels (e.g., "good" and "bad") that evolve through a labeling process; the success of each label depends on the transfer cost associated with it. Crucially, this dynamic is equivalent to a "migrating players game" with two competing populations. Our findings reveal a complex relationship between the topology of labeling and the stability of coexistence: labeling topologies that are both more diverse and more diverse lead to greater stability. This insight is particularly significant for understanding the evolution of linguistic consistency.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have established themselves as a potent tool for addressing forward and inverse challenges within the realm of operational research. However, recent findings indicate that PINNs often fail to learn high-frequency solution components effectively, resulting in subpar performance. This study offers a theoretical explanation for such spectral bias in PINNs and empirically demonstrates that the optimization algorithm can exacerbate the issue. We further propose that incorporating momentum during training serves as an effective remedy to mitigate spectral bias. Empirical results across multiple test cases confirm that the optimized PINNs (OPINN) significantly outperform standard PINNs in both accuracy and computational efficiency. The performance of this enhanced model is validated on a Laplace equation with complex boundary conditions and a Black-Scholes partial differential equation (PDE) involving non-local terms.

This work examines a system coupling a string and an Kelvin-Voigt damped beam through an interface. The strings are not fully damped; Kelvin-Voltov damping occurs only within specific regions. Under suitable initial conditions, we show that total energy dissipates at a polynomial rate. Furthermore, by analyzing how the domain of the underlying operator evolves with the damping parameters, identifying a critical condition for the operator's self-adjointness. This link between the operator structure and the domain of stability is crucial for our analysis. We also establish that the energy decay rate is determined explicitly by the distance between the open set where damping is present and the interface where the strings and beam meet. This work extends previous findings regarding the stability of the system when Kelvin-Voltov damping is present throughout the strings. We also provide numerical simulations to verify our theoretical predictions.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated success across numerous control tasks, yet its deep learning counterparts often function as opaque "black boxes," rendering them unsuitable for safety-critical environments. While model-based RL approaches utilize learned transition models to enhance sample efficiency, they frequently suffer from a lack of interpretability. Consequently, this study introduces a hierarchical RL framework that explicitly leverages interpretability to facilitate human-in-the-loop monitoring and real-time intervention. By integrating a learned black-box model with an interpretable white-box component, the agent can deduce logical explanations for its actions. This approach offers transparency into the reasoning process of the underlying black-box system. To automatically discover these logical rules, we apply inductive logic programming using an explanation-based model, thereby enabling hierarchical reinforcement learning where higher-level agents monitor execution and intervene as needed. Our empirical results validate that this mechanism successfully detects anomalous behaviors and supports timely human intervention.

We propose a quantum compression-based approach to generate optical asymmetry. This method involves a two-mode squeezed state interacting with a single-photon Fock state, which, upon measurement, filters for specific correlations to produce optical asymmetry. We examine how the degree of quantum compression and non-Gaussian characteristics of the Fock state influence these correlations and asymmetries. Our results indicate that lower excitation levels in the Fock state yield stronger correlations accompanied by higher asymmetry values. Additionally, quantum asymmetry can be amplified by optimizing measurement settings. This study suggests that quantum compression serves as a valuable resource for engineering optical asymmetry.

This study examines the extended Fenton problem regarding the estimation of a vector of phase shifts from a set of complex-valued functions. The specific functions considered are polynomials, finite polynomials, and Riemannian translates of a single continuous positive real-valued function. The work addresses both inverse and minimax challenges, providing concrete examples of functions where a linear estimator yields optimal results.

The bosnev experiment has recently reported a new $^{6}$Li-enhanced signal, prompting an investigation into spin-dependent dark matter (DM) interactions. We analyze the impact of this finding on current limits derived from the bosnev data by examining two specific models: one involving a DM scalar interacting with nucleons via a pseudoscalar mediator, and another where the DM spinor couples to nucleons through a pseudoscalar intermediary. Our results indicate that, for these models, the original spin-dependent cross-section limits from bosnev remain largely unaffected by the $^{6}$Li anomaly. However, we demonstrate that the most stringent constraints in these scenarios now originate from the CoGeNT and EDELWEISS experiments.

Blind image restoration aims to recover an image from a single degraded observation while simultaneously estimating the unknown blur kernel. This paper introduces a new method utilizing a kernel mixture model, enhanced by a novel regularizer designed to resolve the inherent ambiguity of blind restoration. The proposed approach models the degraded image as a combination of multiple kernels, each with varying spatial support sizes. A variational Bayesian framework is employed to model the prior distribution of these mixing coefficients, with a regularizer applied to enforce sparsity within the coefficients. Since this blur-kernel mixture structure aligns well with image characteristics at boundaries, it serves as an effective regularizer for the primary restoration term. Experimental results demonstrate that the method outperforms existing techniques in restoring blind images, exhibiting notable advantages in recovering image boundaries and preserving geometric details.

This study demonstrates how a nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation (NYAYE) can be used to construct a new class of dual pairs consisting of (L, R)-infinitesimal dual varieties. These structures serve as a generalization of the previously identified pairings involving (L, R)-infinitesimal dual representations of a nonuniform Yang-Baxter equation (NUYBE) and those arising from the symmetric associative Yang-Baxter equation.

This work addresses reasoning about program correctness within a logical framework that integrates propositional logic with a language designed for natural expression in natural form. In this approach, the state of a program is expressed using time-dependent formulas, where temporal assertions serve as preconditions and postconditions within the context of Hoare logic. We introduce a reasoning methodology that treats temporal formulas as Hoare triples, providing both soundness and completeness. Furthermore, we outline a proof procedure that enables the derivation of program invariants without explicit reference to time. Our methodology is validated through case studies that involve analyzing descriptions of well-known problems, such as finding a maximum value, performing binary search, and reversing a list, to demonstrate its soundness and effectiveness.

This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of the Canopus consensus protocol that ensures resilience against both node crashes and Byzantine faults. While Canopus was originally designed to be crash-tolerant in a static network, RCanopus extends its capabilities to dynamic environments where validators can join or leave, and nodes may exhibit either honest or Byzantine behavior. The new protocol retains Canopus's core advantages, such as minimal memory and network overhead, simplicity, and the ability to reach consensus without waiting for quorum acknowledgments. Notably, RCanopus successfully achieved consensus during the 2017 and 2018 S3 bucket deletion attacks on the Ethereum network.

Lateral lipid segregation within membranes is a widely recognized phenomenon that remains a subject of debate, particularly regarding the role of cholesterol in modulating the bending rigidity of lipid bilayers. To resolve this uncertainty, we conducted extensive molecular dynamics simulations to determine how cholesterol influences the bending modulus of pure DPPC and pure DOPC membranes. Our findings indicate that the bending modulus of DPPC membranes containing cholesterol surpasses that of DPPC alone, whereas DPPC behaves differently compared to DOPC; specifically, the modulus of a cholesterol-containing DOPC membrane is lower than that of a pure DOPC membrane. Furthermore, we analyzed lipid mechanical properties and stress profiles to elucidate the physical mechanisms driving these observations.

We present a framework within loop quantum gravity that coherently unifies the Ashtekar-Lenisson Hamiltonian, the Holomorphic Hamiltonian, and the original formulation. The approach derives each component from an identical underlying Hamiltonian density, which is defined as a function of the curvature of the connection and the spatial metric. By employing the full Poisson bracket structure, the transition rules connecting these three representations to one another are established. The model's consistency is further supported by the existence of a large, continuous set of solutions that satisfy the primary constraints.

The Pierre Auger Observatory, a large-scale instrument dedicated to recording the highest-energy cosmic rays, is currently the leading facility in this field. The Observatory's data regarding these particles are archived in the official Pierre Auger Registry (PAR), a public database accessible at https://www.pierreauger.org/pierreauger-registry. This paper provides an overview of the Pierre Auger Observatory's operational status during Phase I, supported by a detailed analysis of the contents within the PAR. The review covers the registry's structure, the characteristics of the highest-energy events, and the scientific objectives of the Observatory.

Although deep object detectors have achieved remarkable success in accuracy, their inability to assess prediction uncertainty poses a significant challenge for practical applications. This paper introduces a straightforward and computationally efficient method to estimate uncertainty for object detection models without altering their training procedures or architectural designs. By leveraging well-established techniques from Bayesian Deep Learning, the proposed approach utilizes stochastic dropout during inference to generate multiple model samples and calculates statistical moments to quantify uncertainty. Specifically, prediction confidence is determined using the variance of class-conditional probabilities, while predicted bounding box positions are represented as a set of ellipses derived from the first and second-order moments of box distribution parameters. Extensive experiments conducted on the PASCAL VOC 2007 and COCO datasets demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions in both simplicity and overall performance.

Accurate forecasting of traffic flow is essential for efficient urban mobility. While existing models often rely on extensive historical datasets, they frequently fail to account for the inherent characteristics of specific traffic segments. This paper introduces a novel approach for traffic prediction that leverages urban traffic snippets. By utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN), the system extracts salient features from these snippets, while a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network predicts future flow states. This combined architecture effectively captures both spatial and temporal dynamics within traffic data. Experimental evaluations across two real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions.

Accurate quantification of hippocampal subregions is vital for advancing research into epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases. This study introduces a new convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture designed to segment the hippocampus into nine distinct areas within the coronal plane. The network was evaluated on 100 MRI scans obtained from 20 patients with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy (DR-TLE) and 80 scans from 20 individuals diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Quantitative analysis revealed that the proposed method achieved an overall Dice coefficient of 0.954 for hippocampal segmentation and a Dice coefficient of 0.854 for partitioning the structure into nine regions. These results demonstrate that the new method is both efficient and effective.

We investigate the pionhole phenomenon within the context of SGM using the example of transversal modes. In this study, we analyze the distribution of particles across these transversal modes and compare our findings with predictions made by classical statistics. Additionally, we explore how the initial state influences the resulting distribution. Our analysis demonstrates that the fundamental pigeonhole effect emerges from basic quantum principles, meaning it persists even in scenarios lacking particle indistinguishability or statistical correlations. Furthermore, we examine how particle production rates vary with detection time and assess the impact of particle losses on the observed distribution.

The study presents a Monte Carlo simulation designed to model the trajectories of protons from the Cosmic Ray Atmospheric Noise (CRAND) environment that are trapped within the Low Earth Orbit space. The simulation utilizes the latest version of the International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF) model to calculate the Local Magnetic Field, while the Particle Transport code, GEANT4 (version 10.7), simulates the subsequent movement of the protons. The results indicate that the majority of these protons possess an energy level below 100 keV. Additionally, the study analyzes the temporal distribution of the trapped particles, showing a correlation with the Solar Activity Cycle. The findings reveal that the density of these protons is significantly higher within the South Atlantic Magnetic Anomaly (SAA) region. The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of this modeling work.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for processing graph-based data, though their reliance on fixed graph structures restricts their applicability to scenarios lacking such topology. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a neural graph embedding model capable of embedding fixed graphs into a learnable, skeletonized structure, thereby enabling graph-free input processing. We have rigorously evaluated this approach against various neural architectures, demonstrating that our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on benchmark graph prediction tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a graph learning model based on this universal skeleton, which outperforms current methods on the edge prediction problem. Finally, we validate the model's robustness through extensive experiments across a broad spectrum of graph prediction tasks, highlighting its versatility and effectiveness.

This work presents the Huber framework, designed to handle specific vulnerability scenarios within differentially private low-rank matrix fulfillment. We begin by outlining a discrete decision problem domain where differentials privacy constraints are essential, subsequently demonstrating that certain instances of low-rank matrix fulfillment are subject to full privacy risks. Subsequently, we outline an adaptable Huber framework designed to mitigate these vulnerabilities. We then apply this Huber approach to low-rank matrix fulfillment, providing specific instances where the Huber approach offers enhanced utility over purely private alternatives. The simulation of analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) is typically modeled using curves that replicate the latency introduced by ADCs during simulations. This curve delay, often referred to as "aperture time," converts a changing input voltage into a quantized digital value over a finite interval instead of instantaneously. This non-instantaneous conversion creates errors when a changing voltage is sampled, a phenomenon known as aperture uncertainty error. This error can be conceptualized as the averaging of the input voltage over the sampling interval. To accurately simulate this effect, a simulation model must perform a time-integration over the sampling interval. However, since models of individual systems frequently lack the specific time-resolution required for precise integration, approximations are necessary. This paper introduces a method for generating curves that model ADC delay by fitting to the output characteristics of real hardware. Furthermore, it demonstrates that such modeled curves can effectively replace the time-integration approach in simulation models that operate at lower resolution.

We introduce a diagrammatic framework designed to analyze complex multi-photon scattering events within waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED) regimes. This approach is developed for a setup involving two two-level atoms coupled to a one-dimensional lossy transmission line, enabling the calculation of all $2n$-photon input-output amplitudes derived from $n$-photon input fields through the superposition of amplitudes linked to specific atom-cavity interaction diagrams. The computational complexity of determining these amplitudes scales polynomially with both the number of photons involved and the system's configuration. We demonstrate the utility of this method by examining three-photon scattering events that result in the generation of multi-excitation polaritons.

This study explores the connection between dark matter density variations and spin interactions. We introduce a novel framework wherein dark matter couples with gravity through an enhanced, spin-dependent gravitational constant, $G_{\rm spin}$. This mechanism generates substantial local dark matter density enhancements near Earth, significantly boosting direct detection event rates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these elevated densities are transient, fluctuating over cosmological timescales. In response, we propose a remedial strategy to sustain high local dark matter concentrations: endowing dark matter with intrinsic spin. By doing so, the spin-dependent interaction remains constant across the varied masses of dark matter, thereby producing an enhanced gravitational attraction that elevates the local density. The feasibility and broader implications of this approach are examined.

In the following discussion, we examine Faulhaber's formula, which calculates the sum of consecutive $k$-th powers for any integers $k$ and $n$. This approach utilizes Bernoulli numbers and provides multiple proofs, with a specific demonstration provided using Euler's original method.

Traditional non-coherent differential detection for Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM) is favored for its moderate complexity and robustness in highly non-Gaussian noise environments, such as impulsive noise. Nevertheless, its reliance on a short linear filter for differential evaluation limits performance in very low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. This paper introduces a new non-coherent differential detector that leverages the inherent properties of CPM to mitigate this limitation. By extending the observation window to improve SNR, the proposed method matches or surpasses the performance of conventional approaches across a broad spectrum of environments.

Reward signals are indispensable for guiding the learning process of reinforcement agents. However, manually crafting these rewards is notoriously difficult and labor-intensive, often resulting in agents exhibiting off-target behaviors. To address this, we introduce an interactive framework enabling human annotators to derive rewards from clusters of generated trajectories. This approach streamlines feedback by focusing efforts on a limited number of selected groups. Furthermore, we employ a visual interface that renders various trajectory clusters side-by-side, facilitating more intuitive decision-making. Our evaluation across three distinct environments demonstrates that this visual and cluster-based method achieves reward learning performance comparable to that of fully handcrafted rewards.

This study examines nucleon structure within noncommutative QCD spacetime, focusing on how the influence of noncommutativity varies with the quark's longitudinal momentum fraction. We present a method to calculate quark and gluon composition functions in nucleons under noncommutative conditions by leveraging the connection between the matrix element of a local operator and the corresponding operator's renormalization group equation in the conventional commutative framework. Specifically, we derive the quark composition functions in noncommutative spacetime by convolving the parton distribution functions (PDFs) established in standard commutative spacetime with a specific kernel. Our results indicate that the impact of noncommutativity on quark distribution functions is negligible. Furthermore, we derive analytical expressions for the noncommutative contributions to both quark and gluon mean squared radii inside the nucleon.

Frustrated quantum spin systems are notable for supporting various exotic states, including topological ones. We introduce the generalized Toric code, known as the pattern model, and develop a p-spin Hamiltonian that maps to the ground state of the gauge theory. Our research examines a torus-based model featuring two distinct pattern sectors, where frustration allows these sectors to coexist in the vacuum state. By employing duality arguments, we demonstrate that the system exhibits chiral topological edges. Furthermore, we identify a phase transition between a topological phase and a ferromagnetic phase, which occurs as spin frustration is mitigated.

In this paper, we introduce a sigma-model approach to estimate the free energy of random band matrices. Building on this method and the sigma-model unsticking technique previously developed in [arXiv:1906.06075], we analyze the finite free energy of random N-by-N matrices with a band of width W = O(N^b) where 0 < b < 1. Our findings demonstrate that in the regime of 0 < b ≤ 2/3, the free energy remains self-averaging as N approaches infinity. Furthermore, we identify the leading-order term of this free energy, which corresponds to the free energy of a finite rank operator characterized by an effective rank approximately equal to NW.

Understanding conversational context is essential for effective comprehension of dialogues. Traditional models often rely on shallow syntactic structures, which frequently fail to capture the deeper semantic nuances and pragmatic implications inherent in natural language. This paper introduces the Meaning Conversational Concept (MCC) to explicitly represent the underlying meaning of conversations. By leveraging these concepts, we develop the Pre-training Meaning Conversational Concept (MCC-Pre) model, utilizing an objective, meaning-centric approach to learn from large-scale dialogue datasets. Experimental results indicate that our model significantly outperforms existing baselines across various tasks, including task-oriented and open-domain dialogue systems. Specifically, MCC-Pre achieves substantial gains in predicting dialog state machines and identifying the main idea of conversations. These achievements underscore the model's ability to robustly represent the objective meaning of conversations, thereby enhancing overall dialogue comprehension capabilities.

Although significant progress has been made in developing machine learning models, explaining their decisions remains a complex challenge. This study introduces a novel framework for evaluating algorithmic interpretability grounded in human learning processes, specifically by linking the cognitive mechanisms required to understand a model's output to the model's inherent interpretability. We define the upper limit of interpretability as the point where a perfectly efficient learner can deduce the model's logic from limited examples. To operationalize this, we propose a metric that estimates the cognitive complexity necessary for a human to mentally simulate the model without observing actual data. Empirical testing reveals a strong positive correlation between this proposed measure and human performance in model evaluation tasks, thereby substantiating the validity of our learning-centric approach and its potential for future applications.

Anomaly detection (AD) has become a critical field due to the growing need for real-time detection of rare events in complex environments. While the Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithm is a widely adopted and effective solution, it often proves too computationally intensive for resource-constrained systems, such as those used in Industry 4.0 and other IoT applications. To address this gap, this study introduces TiWS-iForest, a lightweight variant designed to maintain iForest's effectiveness in detecting anomalies without incurring the original computational burden. TiWS-iForest operates under two key principles: it utilizes loosely supervised data to bypass the requirement for explicit anomaly labels, and it implements a Tiny ML strategy by combining feature selection with model pruning. Specifically, the approach employs the Fisher Score for feature selection and integrates a TiWS-Isolation Tree (TiWS-IT) that creates a sparser decision tree structure than standard iForest trees. Experimental evaluations on both benchmark datasets and a real-world industrial scenario demonstrate that TiWS-iForest matches the performance of the isolation forest in accuracy while offering significant improvements in efficiency regarding computation, memory usage, and execution time.

This study proposes a new class of distributions to capture the progression of events over time, characterized by a Poisson process where the Lambda-Poisson parameter follows a Pareto distribution. Motivated by reliability research, we employ a Bayesian inference approach using Maximum Posterior Estimation (MPE) to analyze the Pareto Lambda-Poisson model under Type-II censoring. Under this framework, closed-form Bayes estimators are derived for all parameters based on diverse prior distributions. To evaluate the model's performance, a Monte Carlo simulation study is conducted to compute point estimates alongside confidence intervals. The efficacy of the proposed method is further validated through real-world data analysis.

These results confirm the existence of a composition spread among FG stars and demonstrate that the bimodal red MS structure is intrinsic to the SG population rather than a blend of different populations.

Image cataloging is a core component of modern computer vision, with applications spanning object recognition, image retrieval, and visual search. This paper introduces a secure keyless verification method for the classic Shannon model, which features a legitimate sender and receiver connected via an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel and potentially an eavesdropper linked through a weaker version of that same limit. Load balancing is essential for the efficient operation of contemporary cloud infrastructure.
